ch06.title: The Woman at the Well and the Night on Gilboa
ch06.b002: At the end of June, A.D. 27, the thirteen left Jerusalem. Their tents and their few belongings had been sent ahead to be stored at the home of Lazarus in Bethany. The road ran north, toward Samaria. As he walked, Simon Zelotes kept looking back over his shoulder. They were leaving because word had come that the Sanhedrin was again preparing to seize the Master. *Retreating again,* he thought, and swallowed the thought. In his days among the Zealots, a march like this would have had only one name: withdrawal.
ch06.b003: They kept the Sabbath at Bethel, and for several days they taught the people who came over from Gophna and Ephraim. Men from Arimathea and Thamna arrived to ask the Master to visit their villages. For more than two weeks they taught Jews and Samaritans side by side in that region, and some came from as far away as Antipatris. The people of southern Samaria listened gladly.
ch06.b004: That summer Nathaniel watched the faces of his companions slowly change. At first every one of them shrank from dipping his hand into the same dish as a Samaritan. Words heard since childhood clung to the tips of their tongues. But as the days of breaking bread together and drinking from the same jar piled up, those words fell away one by one. It was so with Nathaniel himself. He was, after all, the man who had once asked whether anything good could come out of Nazareth. No one knew better than he how easily a prejudice takes root, and how hard it is to pull out.
ch06.b005: Yet one man stayed exactly as he was. When a Samaritan held out a cup of water, Judas Iscariot took it with only his fingertips. He returned greetings with a smiling face, but his eyes did not smile. Nathaniel saw it and said nothing. Judas was a Judean. Samaria was foreign enough to a Galilean, but to a man raised near Jerusalem it was not merely foreign; it was enemy country. Nathaniel tried to understand him that way. But the harder he tried, the more he felt that something lay between Judas and himself. Judas had never once laughed at any of Nathaniel’s jokes.
ch06.b007: In the last week of July they moved to Phasaelis and Archelais, new Greek cities near the Jordan, and they spent the first half of August there. Hardly any Jews lived in those towns. For the first time the apostles were preaching almost entirely to gentiles—Greeks, Romans, Syrians.
ch06.b008: There Simon became a laughingstock for the first time. He was explaining the kingdom with all his zeal, speaking of turning the other cheek and loving one’s enemies, when a burly Roman folded his arms and laughed. That, he said, was a religion for slaves and weaklings. Simon’s face burned. The words stung because he had once said the same thing himself. In his Zealot days he had sneered at the meek. A man who will not take up the sword, he used to say, can only live as a slave.
ch06.b009: At one of the evening conferences the apostles poured out what they had met with. Philip spoke as if for them all. These Greeks and Romans, he said, scorned their message as fit only for the weak and for slaves. They claimed their own religion made men strong and bold, while this teaching would turn everyone into meek cowards who would soon vanish from the earth. They liked the Master well enough, but they would not take his apostles seriously. What should they say to these gentiles? Thomas and Nathaniel, Simon and Matthew added stories of their own.
ch06.b010: The Master heard them all out and then began to speak. Simon realized at once that his voice was not as usual. He had come, the Master said, to do his Father’s will and to reveal the Father’s love, and that he would do no matter who misunderstood him. Then he asked them: who had told them that his gospel was only for slaves and weaklings? Did they look like weaklings? Had John looked like one? Did he himself seem to them a slave to fear?
ch06.b011: Simon raised his head. He had never once seen this man afraid. When the Pharisees glared at him, when the Sanhedrin sought to arrest him, he did not hurry. That composure was the very thing Simon admired most in him. But he had never thought to call it courage. Courage, to Simon, meant drawing a sword.
ch06.b012: The Master told them not to imagine that the service of the kingdom would be easy and comfortable. Many of them, he said, would be put to death for this gospel. It is easy enough to die in battle with comrades at your side to hold you up; it takes a higher and deeper courage to lay down your life calmly and alone, for love of a truth you carry in your heart. The courage of the body is the lowest kind, he said; bravery of mind is higher; and the highest of all is unwavering loyalty to one’s enlightened convictions about profound spiritual realities. That is the courage of a man who knows God, and they were all men who knew God.
ch06.b013: Simon’s hands trembled. Many times he had dreamed of dying beside his comrades—before the spear points of Roman soldiers, in the midst of a battle cry. To him that was the most glorious death there was. And this man said it was the easiest. Alone, quietly, with no one beside you. Simon had never imagined such a death. When he tried to imagine it now, a chill went down his back. It was more frightening than any fight he had known. And strangely, it rang louder in him than any call he had ever heard.
ch06.b014: It was rare for the Master to speak with such evident feeling. He spoke a long time that night. From then on Simon no longer recited the gentle virtues apologetically when he preached. Neither did the others. A new boldness came into their words. For the first time Simon thought that perhaps a man could fight without taking up a weapon. The thought was still small. But that night he did not throw it away.
ch06.b016: Boldness alone, though, could not carry them through that summer. Nerves among the apostles and the disciples around them were stretched thin. They were not yet used to living and working together, and they clashed more and more with John’s disciples. Dealing with gentiles and Samaritans was a hard trial for men raised as Jews. It was about this time that Andrew asked the Master how John’s self-denial differed from his own teaching of self-control. Jesus answered that John’s was a way of self-examination and self-restraint, while his was a way of self-forgetfulness and self-mastery, of being made new by the spirit. But even that answer did not soothe the frayed nerves of the twelve. Andrew, nearly at his wits’ end, went to the Master.
ch06.b017: Jesus listened to it all and said that a tangle like this, with so many people and so many strong feelings, could not be talked away. He would not step into such troubles. But he invited them to rest with him for three days. And he told Andrew to go to each of his brothers privately and ask: the Master wishes to go up Mount Sartaba to rest; while we are there, shall we agree not to speak of our troubles? Could Andrew count on him to help?
ch06.b018: When Andrew took him aside that evening, Nathaniel assumed he was about to be scolded; Andrew’s face looked that worn. Instead Andrew spoke of going up the mountain and of not raising a single problem for three days. Nathaniel looked at him a moment and said:
ch06.b019: “Chief, you know who’ll be the first to break that promise, don’t you?”
ch06.b020: For the first time Andrew let out a small laugh. They were both thinking of Peter. Watching Andrew laugh, Nathaniel realized it had been weeks since he had made a joke like that. Somewhere among the gentiles his humor had gone into hiding, and only now did he notice it.
ch06.b021: On the way up the mountain, truly, no one mentioned their troubles. Not even Peter. At the top the Master sat them down around him and told them to learn the value of rest and the power of relaxation. Sometimes the best way to solve a tangled problem was to leave it alone for a while. Coming back refreshed, they would meet it with a clearer head and a steadier hand—and often, while they rested, the problem itself would shrink.
ch06.b022: Nathaniel looked around at the faces in the circle. Andrew’s head was full of problems; John was confused in his heart; James was deeply troubled in his soul. Matthew was hard pressed for money, since among the gentiles few gifts came in. Peter was overwrought and more temperamental than usual; Judas was going through one of his spells of touchiness and selfishness. Simon was torn between love of his nation and the teaching that all men are brothers, and Philip was more and more baffled by the way things were going. Thomas was deep in a season of gloom. Only the twins were themselves. They sat in the mountaintop wind, as calm as ever. Nathaniel watched the two of them for a long while, and thought what a heavy load his own philosophy was beside their simplicity.
ch06.b023: The next day the Master gave each of the twelve a topic to talk about, none of them having anything to do with religion. All day long they laughed and chattered over old memories. At noon, when the Master broke bread and even skipped the spoken thanksgiving, the apostles were startled and glanced at one another. They had never seen him neglect such a formality. And no one held it against him. Simon Zelotes, chewing his bread, burst out laughing. The recreation and play of the apostolic company were his charge. Yet all that summer no one had rested less than he. Today the Master was doing his job for him.
ch06.b024: In the afternoon Simon saw Matthew sitting alone in the shade of a rock. Matthew was counting something on his fingers, and when Simon came near he dropped his hands. Simon had heard that offerings were scarce in the gentile towns and that Matthew was struggling. But today was a day for not speaking of such things. Simon hesitated, then sat down beside him.
ch06.b025: “When you sat at the tax booth, who was the funniest customer you ever had?”
ch06.b026: Matthew looked at him in surprise. A Zealot was asking a publican about his days at the customs table—and smiling as he asked. Matthew hesitated a long while, then told of a farmer who had hidden a young goat under his cloak to dodge the toll and was caught when the goat bleated. Simon laughed until he held his sides. Matthew laughed with him. It was the first time the two had ever laughed together. When the laughter died, they sat without speaking and looked down on the Jordan valley as the light faded. Simon did not ask what Matthew had been counting. Matthew did not tell him.
ch06.b027: On the third day, when they came down the mountain, they were changed. They had found out that many of their troubles did not really exist, that much of what pressed on them had been made by exaggerated fear and swollen worry. While they were away, the problems had settled themselves. Back in camp, seeing each other’s faces, several of them laughed out loud. Where had the sharp faces of three days ago gone? Nathaniel laughed loudest of all. From that day, relations with John’s disciples improved markedly.
ch06.b029: On a Monday morning about the middle of August, the Master said to Andrew: we go into Samaria. And they set out at once for Sychar, near Jacob’s well.
ch06.b030: At those words James Zebedee’s stomach turned over. The Greek cities of the Decapolis and Syria were one thing. But the heart of Samaria? For centuries Jews and Samaritans had refused to deal with one another—ever since Assyria had carried off the people of the northern kingdom and planted other nations in their place, ever since the Samaritans had tried to hinder the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile, ever since they had built a temple of their own on Mount Gerizim. James had grown up on those stories. Something rose fiercely in his blood.
ch06.b031: But he got up, and he walked. So did the others. In the year and more they had spent with this man, something had grown in them that was larger than their faith in his teachings and larger than their prejudice against Samaria. If this man went, they went. James could not explain it by reason. His feet simply knew it first.
ch06.b032: When they reached Jacob’s well, the Master, weary from the road, stayed beside the well. Philip took the apostles into Sychar to bring back food and tents, for they meant to stay in that neighborhood for a while. Peter, James, and John said they would remain with the Master. James had no wish to leave him alone in that foreign country. But the Master told them to go with their brothers. They were not to worry about him, he said; these Samaritans would be friendly; it was only their own brethren, the Jews, who sought to harm them.
ch06.b033: James chewed on those last words as he walked into Sychar. The sun was going down. It was nearly six o’clock on that summer evening, and the shadow of Mount Gerizim lay long across the town. The strange Samaritan speech, the strange doorposts, the way the people looked at him. He searched those looks for hostility and did not find it. The bread seller did not cheat him on the price. Somehow that made James angry. It was uncomfortable to feel his reasons for hating disappear one by one.
ch06.b035: They were coming back with bread and dried figs and the tents on their shoulders when someone at the front of the line stopped short. The Master was sitting by the well. And beside him stood a woman—a Samaritan woman. The two of them were alone, close together, deep in conversation.
ch06.b036: The twelve froze where they stood. It was unseemly enough for a man to talk with a woman in a public place. For a Jew to talk with a Samaritan was worse. And here both were happening at once. They hurriedly set down their loads and drew aside. No one dared to reproach the Master. Nathaniel saw James’s jaw tighten. Simon lowered his eyes. Judas turned his face away.
ch06.b037: The Master said to the woman: go your way now; God has forgiven you; from now on you will live a new life, and a new joy will spring up within you. The woman caught the apostles’ disapproval. She left her waterpot where it stood and fled toward the town.
ch06.b038: Nathaniel looked at that waterpot. It was an earthen jar, left standing by itself beside the stone curb of the well. It was half full, and its handle was worn smooth. Some hand had grasped that handle every day, coming and going from this well. And the owner of that hand had just fled because of them. Nathaniel had always thought of himself as the company’s philosopher, a man who had broken his habit of judging people in advance. Yet a moment ago the very same look had come over his face as over the faces of the other eleven. He knew it. The woman had known it too. Nathaniel could not take his eyes off the jar. The proud son of Cana, the man said to be without guile, was ashamed of himself for the first time—before a woman’s waterpot.
ch06.b039: Before the sun went down, a great crowd came streaming out to the well. The woman, whose name was Nalda, had gone into the town telling everyone she met to go out to the well quickly; there was a man there who had told her everything she ever did; could he be the one they were waiting for? The apostles had eaten nothing all day and were hungry. They urged the Master to eat before he spoke to the people. But he knew darkness was coming, and he would not give way. When Andrew pressed him again to take at least a bite, he said he had food to eat that they did not know about.
ch06.b040: The apostles muttered among themselves. Had someone brought him food? Could the woman have given him something to eat as well? James realized his own voice was among the mutterers and shut his mouth. The Master turned to them and said that his food was to do the will of the One who had sent him and to finish his work. Then he raised his hand toward the people coming out of Sychar. Do not say the harvest is still far off, he told them; look, the fields are already white for the harvest. They were being sent to reap what others had labored over. He was speaking of the work of John the Baptist.
ch06.b041: James looked at the people coming toward them in the glow of the evening. Samaritans. The faces he had been taught all his life to hate. Those faces now lay spread out before him like a field of ripened grain. Deep in his chest he heard something give way. Whether it was his anger collapsing, or whatever had been holding his anger up, he could not tell. All he knew was that his fiery temper, for one moment, could find nowhere to go and wandered lost inside him. One day he and his brother would ask to call down fire from heaven on a Samaritan village, as though they had forgotten this evening’s field entirely. Men do not change so easily. But on that one evening James Zebedee stood there, robbed of the strength to hate.
ch06.b042: The next day Nalda came to John and told him the whole story. John never told it fully to the other apostles. Many times he wanted to ask the Master about that day, but he never did. And the Master never spoke of it in detail to the twelve.
ch06.b044: They preached in Sychar for two days and then pitched camp on Mount Gerizim. Many in Sychar believed and asked for baptism, but the apostles were not yet baptizing.
ch06.b045: On the first night at the Gerizim camp the twelve waited to be rebuked. The Master could not have missed the faces they had shown at the well. Simon sat by the fire, bracing himself for a reprimand. It would be a deserved one. But the Master did not say a word about it. Instead he spoke of what truly lies at the center of the kingdom of God. Just as he was to them a brother and friend, he said, he wanted all men to know God as a Father and friend. Love, he told them, was the greatest relationship in the whole universe.
ch06.b046: For the first time Simon learned that a rebuke withheld can hurt more than a rebuke given. Among the Zealots a man who blundered was shouted at, and once he had been shouted at, it was over. But this man did not shout. He waited until they saw it for themselves. Before that waiting, Simon thought again of the eyes he had lowered at the well.
ch06.b047: They stayed on Mount Gerizim until the end of August. By day they went down into the Samaritan towns to proclaim the good news that God is a Father; at night they climbed back to camp. On the ridge lay the ruins of the old Samaritan temple. At the evening gatherings the Master taught them a great deal about worship and prayer. Worship, he said, must alternate with service, and work with play; religion should be balanced by humor, and deep philosophy relieved by poetry.
ch06.b048: At that, Nathaniel stole a glance at Simon. Simon was looking at him. The man in charge of play and the man in charge of jokes. Both looked away at the same instant, and at the same instant both failed to hold back their laughter. The apostles did not understand all that was taught on those nights. Nor did they know that one day, on the site of this ruined temple, Philip would hold many meetings for the Samaritans. But the souls they gathered in Samaria that summer became the field for that later work.
ch06.b050: They spent September and October at a secluded camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa. The religious rulers in Jerusalem were hostile, and Herod still held John in prison. As believers multiplied, tension with John’s disciples grew too. The Master told them plainly that they were in retirement to strengthen their faith, to let the opposition die down, and to await the fate of John.
ch06.b051: That September they rested, talked, and went back over everything since the day they were first called. Each of them dimly sensed that this would be the last chance for a long rest. But none of them had any settled idea of what the kingdom would look like when it came. John and Andrew said it had already come; Peter and James said it had not yet come. Nathaniel and Thomas frankly admitted they did not know. Matthew, Philip, and Simon changed their minds back and forth. The twins did not even know there was an argument. Judas Iscariot said nothing.
ch06.b052: On Gilboa the Master told the apostles much about his early life and his days on Mount Hermon. He also revealed something of what had happened in the hills during the forty days after his baptism. And he charged them plainly to tell no one of these things until he had returned to the Father. Nathaniel treasured those nights. To a philosopher, these were stories more precious than any book. As he listened he pictured to himself the smell of wood shavings in a Nazareth workshop, the snows of Hermon, the solitude of the wilderness. While he listened to those stories, he kept his jokes to himself. And he buried what he heard in his heart. The command to keep silent did not weigh on him at all. Some things are so precious, he felt, that every telling would make them smaller.
ch06.b053: Much of the time the Master was alone on the mountain near the camp. Now and then he took Peter, James, or John with him. James never forgot those nights. The Master almost never prayed aloud. The three of them sat near him and never once heard what he prayed. But when the night grew deep and James looked at his outline against the dark, he thought he knew for whom the Master was sitting there. He asked very little for himself. He spent those long nights on the mountain praying mostly for his disciples, and above all for the twelve. Knowing that was enough to take James’s breath away. Down in the tents below, the other nine slept on, not knowing that someone was keeping watch for them.
ch06.b054: Prayer and worship were the center of their talk that month. After many days of it, Thomas asked the Master to teach them how to pray, and one afternoon in the third week the Master taught them at length. He told of a neighbor who goes at midnight to borrow bread. He asked what father would give his son a stone when the boy needed a loaf. He told of a judge who feared neither God nor man yet granted a widow’s plea because she would not stop pestering him—and said that persistence in prayer is not meant to change the Father but to change ourselves, to enlarge our capacity to receive the spirit.
ch06.b055: Still the apostles wanted a form to teach the believers. James spoke up. That was very good, he said, but what they needed was not a prayer for themselves so much as one for the new believers, who kept begging to be taught how to pray to the Father in heaven. The Master looked at him a moment and said that, if they still wished it, he would give them the prayer he had taught his own brothers and sisters in Nazareth.
ch06.b056: James’s heart lurched. The brothers and sisters in Nazareth—the faces that had not come to the yard at Bethsaida. Long ago, as the eldest son in a fatherless house, this man had sat his little brothers and sisters down in the evenings and taught them this prayer. Those brothers and sisters now misunderstood him and had turned their backs. And yet here he was, taking out the prayer he had taught them and handing it, without a trace of bitterness, to strangers. A prayer that began with the Father in heaven, asked for tomorrow’s bread, asked that the soul be refreshed with the water of life, and asked to be forgiven as we have already forgiven others.
ch06.b057: At that point James bowed his head. Forgiveness came hard to him. Once his anger rose, nothing could hold it, and when the storm had passed he would comfort himself that it had been righteous anger. *As we have forgiven.* Before it was a request made to the Father, those words were a mirror held up to his own face. The bread seller in Sychar, the woman at the well, the Samaritans coming toward him in the sunset. He remembered that evening when he had lost the strength to hate, and for the first time he wondered whether that had been the beginning of forgiveness. Of all the apostles, Peter and James came nearest to understanding the Master’s teaching on prayer and worship. But James himself could not have said, that autumn, what it was he had understood. He only recited the prayer to himself, alone, every night.
ch06.b058: The Twenty-Four, and One Man’s Death
ch06.b059: Around the beginning of October, Philip and some of the other apostles went to a nearby village to buy food and in the marketplace ran into some of the apostles of John the Baptist. John too had recently appointed twelve apostles, at Abner’s urging. That chance meeting led to a three-week conference at the Gilboa camp. Twenty-four men met three times a day, six days a week. Andrew and Abner took turns presiding.
ch06.b060: During the first week the Master mingled with them between sessions, but he firmly refused their request that he preside. He spoke to them only three times, on sympathy, co-operation, and tolerance. When they brought their problems to him, he told them that if any of them had a personal difficulty in his relation to God, he could come at any time; but the ordering of their shared religious life was theirs to decide. If they all agreed, he promised his full support in advance. Then he said he would leave them for two weeks. They were not to worry; he would come back; he would be about his Father’s business, for there were other realms besides this one.
ch06.b061: Simon watched the Master’s back as he went down the slope. For two full weeks they did not see him. Where he went and what he did, they never learned. At first the twenty-four were so unsettled by his absence that they could not get down to business. But within a week they were deep in their discussions again. Simon showed all his skill in those sessions. He loved an argument. But for the first time he learned to argue not in order to win, but in order to reach a conclusion together. They differed, debated, contended, prayed, and gave ground.
ch06.b062: They agreed that both groups would teach believers the prayer the Master had given them. As long as John lived, each apostolic company would carry on its own work, but they would meet together every three months. Baptism was the hardest question. They decided that while John lived, only John’s apostles would baptize, and the Master’s apostles would instruct. If John died, his apostles would come to the Master and place themselves under his direction. On the last afternoon, just as they finished with the question of money, the Master returned. He listened to all their decisions and said that these, then, were their conclusions, and he would help each of them carry out the spirit of what they had decided together. The Gilboa camp was broken up on November 2.
ch06.b063: Through November and December the twenty-four worked quietly in the Greek cities of the Decapolis—Scythopolis, Gerasa, Abila, and Gadara. One of the Master’s apostles went out with one of John’s; John’s apostle baptized, and the Master’s apostle taught. Simon too was paired with one of John’s men. For the first few days the two eyed each other warily, but soon they were arguing late into the night over the law and the kingdom. As time went on, John’s apostles came to understand why the Master did not visit John in prison or try to free him. But they never understood why he worked no great wonders. Neither did Simon.
ch06.b064: At the end of December they moved near Pella. One afternoon some of John’s friends arrived bearing a last question from the prison: was he truly the one, or should they look for another? The Master broke off his teaching and told them to go back and tell John that he was not forgotten, to tell him what they had seen and heard, that good news was being preached to the poor. Then he told the crowd that John was no reed shaken by the wind, and that among those born of women none was greater. John did not ask out of doubt, he said, but to steady his disciples.
ch06.b065: Simon thought of the dungeon at Machaerus. A desert fortress, a year and a half of darkness. Inside it a man was still asking about the kingdom. One sentence—*you are not forgotten*—would go all the way down into that darkness. Simon could not tell whether such words could be stronger than a sword, or whether, having no sword, this was all they could send. The messengers talked with Abner and then left for Machaerus. Later word came that John had been greatly comforted by what they told him. When Simon heard that, it seemed to him that he had found the answer to his own question. A single sentence could raise a prisoner to his feet.
ch06.b066: On the evening of January 10, A.D. 28, John was beheaded by order of Herod. His disciples claimed the body and buried it at Sebaste, Abner’s home, and on January 12 they started north to Pella with the news. The Master dismissed the crowd and called the twenty-four together. John was dead, he told them; Herod had beheaded him. Tonight they should meet in joint council and put their affairs in order. There would be no more delay. The hour had come to proclaim the kingdom openly and with power. Tomorrow they would go into Galilee.
ch06.b067: Simon felt as if his chest would burst. *With power.* He had waited a year and a half to hear those words. John’s blood had at last roused this man. He clenched his fist. But inside that fist, along with everything else, he was holding the words from that summer night in the Greek cities: that the highest courage is not the sword but loyalty that holds to the end. Simon did not know how both could fit in one hand. Early on the morning of January 13, the Master and the apostles, with about twenty-five other disciples, set out for Capernaum. Simon walked at the very front.
ch06.b069: The events follow Papers 143 and 144: leaving Jerusalem at the end of June and teaching at Bethel, Gophna, Ephraim, Arimathea, and Thamna, with Judas alone finding it hard to love the Samaritans (143:0.1–0.3); Philip’s question at Phasaelis and Archelais, the address on courage, and the change in the apostles’ preaching (143:1.1–1.9); Andrew’s question on self-denial and self-control (143:2.2); the three days on Mount Sartaba, the state of each of the twelve, the omitted thanksgiving, and the laughter on return (143:3.1–3.8); the old enmity with the Samaritans and the apostles’ loyalty (143:4.1–4.3); Jacob’s well and the apostles sent into Sychar, Nalda and the abandoned waterpot, the crowd before sundown, the words on food and harvest, and Nalda’s account to John (143:5.1–6.1, 143:5.12–5.13); the camp on Mount Gerizim, the first night without rebuke, and the teaching on worship (143:6.2–7.9); the retirement on Gilboa and its reasons, the apostles’ views of the kingdom, the account of his early life and the forty days under a charge of silence, and Jesus alone in prayer (144:0.1–1.8); the discourse on prayer, James’s request, the prayer taught in Nazareth, Peter and James as those who understood best, and the night prayers for the twelve (144:1.9–4.11); the conference of the two apostolic groups, the two weeks of absence, and the agreements (144:6.1–6.13); the paired work in the Decapolis (144:7.1–7.4); John’s question, Jesus’ answer, and John comforted (144:8.1–8.7); John’s execution and the departure for Galilee (144:9.1–9.2). The wish of James and John to call down fire on a Samaritan village (139:3.5) and Philip’s later work in Samaria (143:4.2, 143:6.6) are used as foreshadowing.
ch06.b070: Character facts come from Paper 139: Nathaniel’s pride and humor (139:6.3–6.4) and Judas’s disapproval of him (139:6.5); James Zebedee’s fiery temper and his excuses for it (139:3.2); Simon Zelotes as head of recreation, his Zealot past, his admiration for Jesus’ poise, and his love of debate (139:11.1–11.6); the simplicity of the twins (139:9.2).
ch06.b071: Fiction has been added in the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings, in landscape and weather, the Roman who mocked Simon, the brief joke between Nathaniel and Andrew, Simon’s laughter at the mountaintop meal, Simon asking Matthew about his customs days and their shared laughter, the bread seller of Sychar, the look of the waterpot, Nathaniel and Simon’s suppressed laughter on Gerizim, Simon’s debates with his partner in the Decapolis, and Simon walking at the front. The text does not say which apostle first saw Jesus at the well, so it is left as “someone.” The text does not say where Jesus went during his two weeks away, and nothing is invented about it.
ch06.b072: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
